content.overview: A proposal (offer) when accepted becomes a promise. Communication, revocation, and acceptance rules under sections 3–9 determine when parties are bound.

sections.heading: Statutory scope — Offer and acceptance — ICA ss. 2–9
sections.body: This topic is confined to the identified statutory provisions. The statutory text and the specific legal effect of each provision should control the analysis.

sections.heading: Communication and revocation
sections.body: Communication of proposal, acceptance, and revocation follows sections 3–5. A proposal may be revoked before acceptance is complete as against the proposer. Acceptance must be absolute and unqualified (s. 7).

illustrations: A posts a proposal to sell goods and B posts an unconditional acceptance; the legal effect is determined by sections 3–7 on communication, completion, revocation and absolute acceptance.

learningObjectives: Explain how communication of proposal, acceptance and revocation operates under ICA ss.3-5.
Apply the rule for communication and completion of proposals and acceptance.
Distinguish revocation from lapse and identify when revocation is too late.
Apply s.7's requirement that acceptance be absolute and unqualified.
Apply s.8 where conduct or performance constitutes acceptance.
Recognise express and implied promises under s.9.
enhancement.definition: ICA ss.3-9 regulate the communication, completion and revocation of proposals and acceptances and recognise acceptance by performance and express or implied promises. They determine when the parties' communications acquire legal effect.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: Formation is tested provision-by-provision: identify the proposal, determine how and when communication occurred, apply the completion rules, test whether revocation was effective before completion, and require absolute and unqualified acceptance unless the Act recognises acceptance through performance.
statutoryFramework: Indian Contract Act, 1872 — s.3: communication, acceptance and revocation.
Indian Contract Act, 1872 — s.4: communication when complete.
Indian Contract Act, 1872 — s.5: revocation of proposals and acceptances.
Indian Contract Act, 1872 — s.6: modes of revocation.
Indian Contract Act, 1872 — s.7: acceptance must be absolute and unqualified.
Indian Contract Act, 1872 — s.8: acceptance by performing conditions or receiving consideration offered with a proposal.
Indian Contract Act, 1872 — s.9: express and implied promises.
essentialIngredients: A proposal or acceptance must be identified before its communication can be tested.
Determine the legally relevant mode of communication under s.3.
Apply s.4 separately to the proposer and acceptor to determine when communication is complete.
Check whether revocation occurred before the legally relevant completion point under s.5 and s.6.
Test whether acceptance is absolute and unqualified under s.7.
Where applicable, test whether conduct or performance amounts to acceptance under s.8.
Classify the resulting promise as express or implied under s.9.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 3 provides the statutory modes through which proposal, acceptance and revocation are communicated. Section 4 then fixes the point at which communication becomes complete: the rule differs depending on whether the communication concerns a proposal, an acceptance or a revocation and whether the relevant party is the proposer or acceptor. Section 5 permits revocation only within the statutory time window; an attempted revocation after the relevant completion point is ineffective. Section 6 identifies recognised modes of revocation, including notice of revocation, lapse of prescribed or reasonable time, failure of a condition precedent and death or insanity of the proposer when known to the acceptor before acceptance. Section 7 requires acceptance to correspond with the proposal and not introduce a new or qualified bargain. Section 8 recognises conduct that performs the conditions of a proposal, or acceptance through receipt of the consideration offered with it, as acceptance. Section 9 distinguishes express promises, communicated in words, from implied promises arising from conduct or circumstances. These provisions should be read together rather than treated as isolated rules.
examples: A posts an offer and B posts an unconditional acceptance. The answer must identify the statutory completion rules before deciding when the agreement arose.
A attempts to revoke an offer after acceptance has already become complete against A under the applicable communication rule. The revocation is too late.
A proposal invites acceptance by performing a specified act. B performs that act in accordance with the proposal; s.8 may treat the conduct as acceptance.
A responds to an offer by changing the price or adding a new condition. The response is not an absolute and unqualified acceptance under s.7.
distinctions: Communication of a proposal vs communication of acceptance: s.4 applies different completion points.
Revocation vs rejection: revocation is withdrawal by the proposer or other statutory mode; a counter-proposal is not an absolute acceptance.
Absolute acceptance vs qualified acceptance: adding a new term generally prevents the response from being acceptance under s.7.
Express promise vs implied promise: s.9 turns on whether the promise is made in words or inferred from conduct/circumstances.
problemApplication: Step 1: identify the proposal and the exact terms offered.
Step 2: identify the alleged acceptance and whether it is absolute and unqualified.
Step 3: map each communication to s.3 and determine completion under s.4.
Step 4: place any revocation on the same timeline and test it under ss.5-6.
Step 5: if acceptance is by conduct, test s.8.
Step 6: classify the promise under s.9 and state whether an agreement has been formed on the stated facts.
keyTakeaways: Sections 3-6 are primarily timing and communication rules.
Section 7 protects the requirement of absolute and unqualified acceptance.
Section 8 recognises acceptance through specified performance.
Section 9 distinguishes express and implied promises.
The chronology of communications is often decisive.
